newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi held in Canada says no Iran links - group.
newsitem.headline: Saudi held in Canada says no Iran links - group.

text.p: A Saudi dissident held in Canada for an alleged role in a bombing that killed 19 U.S. airmen in Saudi Arabia has told a Moslem human rights group he was opposed to his government and had studied in Iran but had no links to the Tehran government or the blast, the group said on Sunday.

Hani Abdel-Rahim Hussein al-Sayegh also told the London-based Islamic Observation Centre in a telephone call from Ottawa on Thursday that he was not a member of the Saudi Hizbollah group and that he agreed to be tried publicly in Canada but would not deal with any U.S. interrogators.
"Al-Sayegh said he was an opponent of the Saudi government but he denied any ties to the bombing and said he was not a member of Saudi Hizbollah," a spokesman for the group told Reuters.
"He said he had spent time in Iran for religious studies but said he had no political or organisational relations with the Iranian government," the spokesman added.
Iran's embassy in Ottawa has issued a statement denying any links with Sayegh, a 28-year-old Shi'ite Moslem, or the bombing.
The spokesman said Sayegh had contacted the group's Canada representative on Thursday from prison and was connected to its London office in a conference call.
The Islamic Observation Centre advocates human rights for Moslems around the world and also monitors media reports.
The Canadian government on Thursday charged that Sayegh, one of two Saudi dissidents it is holding, was a driver involved in the truck bomb that killed 19 U.S. servicemen in Saudi Arabia last June.
In documents filed with the Federal Court, Canada's intelligence service alleged that Sayegh conducted surveillance at the site of the bombing, which also wounded about 400 people.
It said he then drove a car which "signalled the explosives-laden truck to enter the parking lot".
Sayegh was arrested in Ottawa on March 18 on the grounds that he represented a security threat to Canada.
The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation has said it wanted to put questions about the bombing to Sayegh, who denies being in Saudi Arabia last June.

"Sayegh said he refuses to deal with American interrogators because of its policy against Moslems aimed at destroying the reputation of Islam, including its use of the veto against the U.N. resolution against Israeli settlements," said the spokesman.
"He said he is willing to be tried in any open court outside the United States and Saudi Arabia," he added.

The document filed by the Canadian government with the court said the Canadian Security Intelligence Service had reasonable grounds to believe that Sayegh was a member of Saudi Hizbollah or Hizbollah al-Hijazi.
It described this entity as being born of the fundamentalist group Hizbollah -- which means Party of God -- based in Lebanon.
Sayegh has said he was in Syria at the time of the bombing at the Khobar Towers, a complex housing U.S. military personnel outside Dhahran in the oil-rich eastern part of Saudi Arabia.
He arrived in Canada on a flight that stopped in Boston. It was conceivable Canada could use that as a reason to deport him to the United States if he were found to be a security risk.
A second Saudi, Fahad al-Shehri, is being held in the same Ottawa prison on charges of "terrorism", which he denies.
